Notebook.Title: Advanced Sia and Std: Reactors, Events, Concurrency, and Serialization

Section.Title: What std means in this repository
Section.Paragraph: Sia's standard-library package is currently named Sia.Prelude. It builds on the core ECS with reusable Sia.Reactors services and the Sia.Reactive reconciliation runtime. This notebook also covers three core boundaries: events can be intercepted without sender and handler coordinating directly, parallel data work is allowed but structural mutations return to one owning thread, and a world can be frozen to bytes and restored.

Every cell here is an independent scene: run one and only that scene compiles and executes, so the eight of them work in any order. When a scene reuses a component type from another, it declares its own copy.

Section.Title: 1. Std Reactors: hierarchy, aggregation, and stable ids
Section.Paragraph: Reactors are world addons that maintain derived relationships from ordinary components. Hierarchy<TTag> maintains parent/child links, Aggregator<TId> maintains groups, and Mapper<TId> provides an id-to-entity lookup. Your domain data stays small while the addon owns the index.

Disablement propagates downward through every descendant, not just the immediate child — that is why disabling shell alone is enough to make editor report itself disabled too, with no separate write to editor at all.

Section.Title: 2. Std Reactive: describe desired state, then reconcile
Section.Paragraph: A [ReactiveComponent] is a pure description of desired structure plus Hooks. UseState stores component-local state. A flush expands dirty components and reconciles their terms with the existing ECS graph, preserving identity where the shape is compatible and cleaning it up on unmount.

A flush settles on whatever the state holds at that moment, not a log of every update made since the last flush — several calls to Update between two flushes would still only ever produce one reconciled entity.

Section.Title: 3. Higher-order events: cancel, pause, and resume
Section.Paragraph: An event that implements ICancellableEvent, IPausableEvent, or IRevertableEvent can be intercepted by a second event aimed at the same entity, without the original sender or handler knowing about each other. HOEvents.Cancel<TEvent> is the simplest of the three to see end-to-end: a system declares filter: EventUnion.Of<HOEvents.Cancel<TEvent>>() and is skipped entirely for any entity a cancel also arrived for that same tick. The same mechanism backs Pause<TEvent>/Resume<TEvent> (suspend one event type without touching any other system) and Revert<TEvent> (hand a handler the event's previous value).

The filter only ever protects a tick where a matching cancel actually showed up: without that HOEvents.Cancel<SigTerm> send above, SignalTermSystem would have destroyed stubborn-daemon itself, well before the manual Destroy() call even runs.

Section.Title: 4. EventSystemBase: dispatch by type, and remember what changed
Section.Paragraph: SystemBase reacts to a trigger by re-running its whole query. An EventSystemBase instead dispatches per recorded event type through HandleEvent<TEvent> — call RecordEvent<TEvent>() for one event type or RecordEvents<TEventUnion>() for a whole [SiaEvents] group in Initialize. ComponentEventSystemBase<TComponent> goes further: it snapshots the component's value right before each WorldEvents.Add/Set/Remove<TComponent>, so a handler can compare against what came before. (It only sees whole-component replacement — entity.Set(component) — not a single [Sia] field write through a View; TemplateEventSystemBase adds that finer granularity at the cost of a [SiaTemplate] declaration.)

The first "uptime was 0s before this change" line is real, not a bug: creating an entity with Uptime already attached raises Add and Set together, so the very first observation reports the initial value as its own "before" snapshot too. RecordFor's Add/Set/Remove triad is a component lifecycle notification, not a diff guarantee by itself — combine it with your own check when that distinction matters.

RestartHistorySystem batches every event that happened since the last tick and remembers each one's own snapshot in order, not just the most recent write — a third Set in the same tick would produce a third, correctly-ordered "before" line right along with the two already here.

Section.Title: 5. Parallel queries without parallel structural mutation
Section.Paragraph: ForEachOnParallel distributes query work across workers. Treat entity shape as owned mutable structure: gather decisions concurrently, then add/remove components or destroy entities after the parallel callback completes. This keeps the hot computation parallel without racing the World's archetype storage.

The destroyed count itself is deterministic — exactly 32 here, one eighth of the 256 jobs created above. What is not deterministic is the order entities land in _completed from run to run, because the parallel workers race each other to push onto that stack; only the single-threaded cleanup phase afterward is safe to rely on for order.

Section.Title: 6. SubWorld and extract systems: a read model for another thread
Section.Paragraph: SubWorldAddon hands out a second World tagged with a SubWorldContext back to the first. An ExtractSystemBase running in that second world sees a live, read-only IEntityQuery over the parent's data — useful for a system that should react immediately without ever mutating the parent. SnapshotExtractSystem<T> instead copies matching entities into a plain T[] on demand via RunExtract(), so a consumer can read Data on its own cadence — the frozen array a real background thread would poll instead of touching the live world at all.

Every RunExtract() call replaces the Render pane's bars with that frame's numbers, so watching it across all three ticks is watching three frames of "another thread" catching up to the kernel one snapshot at a time. A real caller would run monitorStage on its own background Thread instead of ticking it inline like this cell does — nothing here needs that thread to prove the read model works, and the deterministic single-threaded order is easier to read top to bottom.

The "[live query] sees 3 process(es)" line above always reflects the live world on every frame; the Render pane's bars only move when RunExtract() actually runs. Skip a call to it on some frame and the two would visibly drift apart — which is exactly the decoupling this section exists to demonstrate: a consumer that stops polling just sees a stale frame, never a torn or racing one.

Section.Title: 7. Context<T>: per-thread state without parameter threading
Section.Paragraph: Context<T>.Current is [ThreadStatic]. A ParallelRunner subclass can override RunWorkerThread to plant a distinct value on each worker once at startup; every job that worker ever runs afterward reaches it through Context.Get<T>(), with no parameter threaded through the call. RunnerBarrier.Get() plus WaitAndReturn() is how you block until a batch of jobs finishes.

Which worker picks up which job is scheduler-dependent, so a second run can print the eight lines in a different order — that non-determinism is the point: each worker still finds its own connection waiting, regardless of which jobs it happens to run.

With a single worker, every job would report the same connection id, since there is only one thread alive to hold state on. Don't read anything into which specific number an id turns out to be, though: this constructor hands each spawned thread a loop variable it reads back whenever the OS gets around to actually starting it, so the id a worker sees is a detail of scheduling timing, not a guaranteed 0-based index.

Section.Title: 8. Serialization: freeze a world to bytes, and back
Section.Paragraph: BinaryWorldSerializer<THostHeader, TComponentSerializer> walks every entity host, tags it with a header, and MemoryPack-encodes each component. The plain BinaryWorldSerializer alias pairs a reflection-based header with MemoryPack and needs no setup for built-in primitives or plain unmanaged structs — a component holding a reference type like string needs [MemoryPackable] (or a hand-written MemoryPackFormatter<T>, see Sia.Serialization.Binary) so MemoryPack knows how to write it. This cell freezes a private World it builds itself and shrinks the stream with GZipStream — the browser runtime ships no Brotli support, so plain GZip keeps the round-trip portable.

These component types are defined right here in this cell, yet they survive the round-trip: the reflection header serializer resolves them from the already-loaded program assembly at restore time. Drop [MemoryPackable] from a struct holding a string, though, and nothing throws — MemoryPack silently skips what it doesn't know how to write, so that field would come back an empty string while a sibling component round-trips correctly right next to it. That's exactly why the reflection header alias is meant for prototypes and demos, not the only line of defense in front of data you can't afford to lose quietly.

Section.Title: Where to go next

List.Item: Reactive.ForEach and PatchForEach reconcile keyed collections.
Reactive.On, Provide, and Use connect events and scoped context.
TemplateEventSystemBase<TComponent, TTemplate> plus a [SiaTemplate] declaration adds per-field diffing (SetX-style) on top of section 4's whole-component Add/Set/Remove triad.
Pause<TEvent>, Resume<TEvent>, and Revert<TEvent> round out section 3's higher-order events.

Section.Paragraph: These are composition tools, not replacements for the core model. Prefer the smallest abstraction that expresses ownership clearly: components for data, systems for scheduled behavior, addons for world-scoped services, reactors for maintained indexes, and Reactive for declarative lifecycles.
